name: Lexington
title: Investor Renovation Contractor in Lexington, KY | Genstone
metaDescription: Lexington, KY renovation contractor for investors: Kenwick and Chevy Chase flips, Gardenside rentals, UK-area duplexes, 203(k) and REO across Fayette County.
intro:
Lexington plays by different rules than most Kentucky markets. Since the late 1950s, the city and county have held development inside an Urban Service Boundary to protect the horse farms that surround town, and that line keeps the supply of buildable land tight. The result is a city where older houses inside the boundary hold their value, renovated homes in neighborhoods like Kenwick, Chevy Chase and Bell Court sell to eager owner-occupants, and the University of Kentucky keeps demand for rentals steady close to campus.

Genstone Construction scopes and manages renovations for investors and lenders working Fayette County: flippers restoring 1920s bungalows near downtown, BRRRR and rental investors buying 1950s ranches in Gardenside, Meadowthorpe and Cardinal Valley, small multifamily owners near campus, FHA 203(k) buyers and servicers with the occasional bank-owned home. A free Pre-Offer Rehab Review prices the job before you buy. A designated field manager then runs it with vetted, licensed Bluegrass contractors, handles permits through the Lexington-Fayette Urban County Government and releases draws only for completed work.
housingStock:
Lexington's oldest residential areas ring downtown. Gratz Park and the blocks around it hold Federal and Greek Revival homes from the early 1800s, while the North Side, South Hill, Western Suburb and Bell Court have Victorian, Italianate and Queen Anne houses from the late nineteenth century, many in brick. Shotgun houses and modest cottages appear in historically working-class and Black neighborhoods such as the East End, Smithtown and parts of the North Side, and in pockets near the old railroad lines.

The early twentieth century brought streetcar suburbs with bungalows, foursquares and Tudor and Colonial Revival homes: Kenwick, Mentelle, Woodward Heights, Aylesford near campus, and the larger, more polished houses of Chevy Chase and Ashland Park. Many have full or partial basements, frame or brick construction and original hardwood and trim.

After the Second World War, Lexington filled out with brick and frame ranches in Gardenside, Cardinal Valley, Meadowthorpe, Southland, Lansdowne and Eastland, many on crawlspaces or basements. Later decades added split-levels, townhomes and subdivisions toward Tates Creek, Hartland, Hamburg and Masterson Station, all inside the service boundary.

The Inner Bluegrass sits on limestone with karst features, which means sinkholes, shallow bedrock in places and fissures that route water in unpredictable ways. Basements can hit rock, foundations may sit on fractured stone and drainage near a sinkhole needs care. Prewar houses carry the usual era items, including knob-and-tube wiring, galvanized supply lines, cast-iron and clay drains, old boilers and lead paint. Post-war homes bring asbestos flooring, original panels and aging ductwork. Across eras, humid summers and clay-rich soils make crawlspace and basement moisture a regular part of the scope, and Lexington's mature street trees add root intrusion into old sewer laterals to the list of things worth checking before you buy.

commonIssues.title: Karst, sinkholes and shallow limestone
commonIssues.body: Fayette County is known for karst geology, and sinkholes and depressions are mapped throughout the area. Homes near a sinkhole may experience drainage problems, settlement or water that disappears into the ground and reappears in a basement. Shallow bedrock can also complicate excavation for footings, sewer work or basement waterproofing. We check property location against mapped karst features, look for cracks and settlement patterns and bring in an engineer when movement appears active rather than old and stable.

commonIssues.title: Wet basements and crawlspaces on clay
commonIssues.body: Lexington's clay-rich soils hold water against foundations after heavy spring rains, and humid summers keep crawlspaces damp. Older homes in Kenwick, Mentelle and the North Side often show efflorescence, seepage, musty odors and rot in sills and joists. The fix starts outside with grading, gutters and downspout extensions, then moves inside to crack repair, drainage, sump pumps, vapor barriers and dehumidification. Sealing interior walls without correcting the water source is a shortcut we often see on past renovations.

commonIssues.title: Sanitary sewer backups and old laterals
commonIssues.body: Lexington has spent years upgrading its sanitary sewer system under a federal consent decree, but older neighborhoods still have clay and cast-iron laterals that crack, sag or fill with roots. During heavy storms, homes with floor drains or downspouts tied into the sewer can see backups. We recommend a camera inspection on prewar purchases, and our scopes may include lateral repair or lining, backwater valves and downspout disconnection where the risk warrants it.

commonIssues.title: Heavy student wear near campus
commonIssues.body: Houses close to the University of Kentucky, including parts of Aylesford, Columbia Heights, Pralltown and the streets off Euclid and Limestone, often show years of student-rental wear: damaged doors and trim, worn floors, abused kitchens and baths, overloaded circuits and unpermitted bedroom conversions in basements and attics. Some were split into units without approval. We document what is legal and what is not, check egress in every bedroom and plan durable finishes that will survive the next round of leases.

commonIssues.title: Lead paint, asbestos and old heating systems
commonIssues.body: Lexington's prewar homes almost always contain lead-based paint on windows, trim, porches and siding, and many 1950s through 1970s homes have asbestos in floor tile, duct wrap or ceiling texture. Federal lead-safe renovation rules apply to pre-1978 houses, and suspect asbestos materials need testing and licensed abatement before demolition. Older homes may also have boilers or converted gravity furnaces. We sequence testing early and decide whether to keep or replace heating systems before walls are opened.

investorMarket:
Because the Urban Service Boundary limits outward growth, Lexington's older neighborhoods inside the line tend to see steady demand, and renovated homes there often sell to owner-occupants. Kenwick, Chevy Chase, Bell Court, Mentelle, Woodward Heights, Castlewood and North Limestone are popular with buyers who want walkable streets, older homes and quick access to downtown and campus. Flips in those areas can justify quality finishes when structure and systems are handled correctly.

Post-war neighborhoods such as Gardenside, Cardinal Valley, Meadowthorpe, Southland, Lansdowne and Eastland are buy-and-hold favorites. Brick ranches and modest homes there rent steadily and appraise predictably, which makes them good candidates for single-family rental and BRRRR strategies.

The University of Kentucky shapes the market around campus, where duplexes, small multifamily buildings and single-family rentals serve students, staff and medical center employees. Zoning, occupancy rules, parking and neighborhood expectations need careful attention there.

Newer subdivisions toward Hamburg, Masterson Station, Hartland and Tates Creek mostly attract owner-occupants and longer-term rental owners rather than heavy rehab work. Bank-owned and distressed properties are less common in Lexington than in some Kentucky cities, so when they appear they often draw competition. The free Pre-Offer Rehab Review helps you compare realistic repair costs with nearby values and rents, so you can decide quickly and confidently.
permits:
Building permits and inspections in Lexington and Fayette County are handled by the Lexington-Fayette Urban County Government's Division of Building Inspection. Work that typically needs a permit includes structural changes, foundation repair, additions, decks and porches, new or relocated plumbing, electrical service upgrades and new circuits, HVAC replacement, demolition and many roofing projects. Kentucky licenses electricians, plumbers and HVAC contractors through the state Department of Housing, Buildings and Construction, and some trade permitting and inspection may run through state-level programs as well as the local building office.

The Division of Code Enforcement enforces property maintenance standards and handles vacant, nuisance and unsafe structures, so open cases should be reviewed before purchase. Lexington protects many older neighborhoods through H-1 historic overlay zoning, including districts such as Gratz Park, Bell Court, South Hill, Aylesford and Elsmere Park. Exterior changes in those districts generally need a Certificate of Appropriateness, reviewed by staff or the Board of Architectural Review, before work begins. Our field managers sort out which reviews apply, pull permits, schedule inspections and collect lien waivers so the renovation file is complete for sale, refinance or rental compliance.
climate: Central Kentucky has humid summers, variable winters and an active spring storm season. Summer heat and humidity drive heavy air conditioning use and keep crawlspaces damp, which feeds mold, rot and termite activity. Paint, drywall and flooring adhesives cure slowly in houses without working HVAC. Winters bring freeze-thaw cycles and occasional ice storms that damage gutters, roofs and trees, along with stretches of cold that can freeze plumbing in vacant homes. Spring rains test basements and drainage, especially near karst features where water can travel unexpectedly, and severe thunderstorms bring wind and hail. We schedule masonry, roofing and exterior paint for the drier parts of late spring and fall, and keep interior trades moving year-round once power, water and climate control are in place.

faqs.q: Does Genstone work in Georgetown, Nicholasville and other Bluegrass towns?
faqs.a: Yes. We coordinate renovations across the Bluegrass region, including Georgetown, Nicholasville, Versailles, Winchester, Paris, Richmond and Wilmore. Each county and city has its own building office, while trade licensing runs through the state. Your field manager confirms the right jurisdiction during scoping, so permits, inspections and contractor requirements are routed correctly for each property, wherever it sits around Fayette County.

faqs.q: How does the Urban Service Boundary affect investors?
faqs.a: The boundary limits outward development, which keeps land inside the line in demand. For investors, that tends to support values in older neighborhoods and makes well-renovated homes attractive to owner-occupants. It also means distressed properties draw competition, so the time between finding a house and making an offer is often short. The free Pre-Offer Rehab Review is designed to give you a realistic repair budget quickly.

faqs.q: Should I worry about sinkholes when buying in Lexington?
faqs.a: It is worth checking, not panicking. Karst features are common in Fayette County, and many homes sit near mapped sinkholes without trouble. The concern is drainage and settlement. We look at the property's location, the condition of the foundation and how water moves around the house. If we see active movement or unusual drainage, we recommend an engineer's review before you commit to the purchase.

faqs.q: Can you manage a Lexington renovation if I live elsewhere?
faqs.a: Yes. Many of our Lexington clients invest from Louisville, Cincinnati or out of state. Your field manager walks the house, sends the written scope with photos, posts progress and milestone documentation, and releases draws only after each stage is complete. Final billing comes after you review and approve the finished work, so you can oversee the project without regular trips to Fayette County.

fix-flip.title: Fix and Flip Contractor in Lexington, KY | Genstone
fix-flip.metaDescription: Lexington fix and flip renovations in Kenwick, Chevy Chase, Mentelle and North Limestone: bungalows rebuilt behind the walls and finished to Fayette comps.
fix-flip.h1: Fix and Flip Renovations in Lexington
fix-flip.intro: Lexington's tight housing supply gives flippers a real advantage when they buy well and renovate carefully. Buyers competing for a renovated bungalow in Kenwick, a foursquare in Mentelle or a brick cottage in Castlewood want original character, a modern kitchen, updated baths and central air. They also want a dry basement and a clean inspection, and Lexington inspectors know where older Bluegrass homes hide problems. Genstone Construction scopes Lexington flips from the foundation up. Our free Pre-Offer Rehab Review prices structure, drainage and systems first, then matches finishes to recent sales on that street. A designated field manager coordinates trades, LFUCG permits and any historic review, keeping your holding costs under control.

sections.h2: What Lexington buyers expect in a renovated older home
sections.body:
In Kenwick, Mentelle, Woodward Heights and Chevy Chase, buyers often compare a flip against carefully restored homes nearby. Refinished hardwood floors, original trim and built-ins where they survive, period-appropriate lighting, a functional kitchen with quality counters and at least one updated bath are common expectations. Front porches matter in these neighborhoods, and a well-rebuilt porch with proper railings and columns can add real appeal.

In North Limestone and Castlewood, buyers may be more focused on condition, layout and price, but they still respond to character and curb appeal. Post-war homes in Meadowthorpe or Southland compete mainly on updated systems, clean finishes and a sound roof.

We review recent sales on the specific street and recommend finishes that match what buyers there have actually paid for. When the comps support more than one path, we can price two finish levels with separate ARV estimates. That helps you decide whether extra spending on tile, cabinetry or lighting is likely to come back at closing or simply reduce your margin.

sections.h2: Foundations, drainage and systems in Lexington flips
sections.body:
Many Lexington flips succeed or fail below the first floor. Older homes in Kenwick and the North Side often have stone or block foundations with seepage, cracks or settlement. Homes near karst features can have drainage that behaves unpredictably. Clay-rich soils hold water after heavy rain, and crawlspaces stay damp through humid summers.

We address those issues before cosmetic work. Typical items include grading corrections, gutter and downspout repairs, crack sealing, drainage systems, sump pumps, crawlspace vapor barriers and structural repairs where joists or sills have rotted. An engineer reviews any foundation movement that looks active.

Systems come next. Older Lexington homes commonly need electrical service upgrades and rewiring to replace knob-and-tube circuits, new supply plumbing, a camera inspection of the sewer lateral and either a new HVAC system or a carefully evaluated boiler. Lead-safe practices apply to windows, trim and exterior work on pre-1978 homes. Taking care of those items produces a cleaner inspection report and protects your sale price.

sections.h2: Historic overlays and scheduling on Lexington flips
sections.body:
Lexington's H-1 historic overlay districts cover several neighborhoods popular with flippers, including Bell Court, South Hill, Aylesford and Elsmere Park. Exterior work there usually needs a Certificate of Appropriateness before it starts. That affects windows, doors, siding, porches, roofing materials and additions, and getting it wrong can mean undoing finished work.

We check every property against overlay maps before the scope is final. If the house is in a district, we plan exterior changes to fit the guidelines and submit for review at the start of the project so it does not hold up the schedule. Interior work generally proceeds without overlay review.

Timing matters for holding costs. Permit applications go to the Division of Building Inspection as soon as the scope is approved, long-lead items such as windows, cabinets and HVAC equipment are ordered early, and trades are sequenced so rough inspections happen promptly. We plan roofing, masonry and exterior paint for the drier parts of the year. Your field manager posts progress so you can schedule listing photos and staging around a realistic finish date.

faqs.q: Which Lexington neighborhoods are strongest for flips?
faqs.a: Kenwick, Chevy Chase, Bell Court, Mentelle, Woodward Heights, Castlewood and North Limestone tend to have strong owner-occupant demand for renovated older homes. Post-war areas such as Meadowthorpe and Southland can also work at a different price point. Results vary block by block, so we check recent sales on the specific street during the Pre-Offer Rehab Review before recommending a scope.

faqs.q: Do Lexington historic districts slow down flips?
faqs.a: They can if exterior work is not planned early. In H-1 overlay districts, changes to windows, siding, porches, roofing and additions usually need a Certificate of Appropriateness before work begins. We identify overlay status before the scope is final and submit for review at the start of the project, so interior work continues while the exterior approval moves forward. Staff-level approvals for routine repairs are often quicker than a full board hearing.

faqs.q: How do you handle basement water on a Lexington flip?
faqs.a: We start outside with grading, gutters and downspouts, then deal with cracks, drainage and sump systems inside. Homes near karst features or with active settlement get an engineer's review. Buyers in Lexington often ask about basement water, so we document the repairs with photos and receipts that your listing agent can share during showings and negotiations. That record often heads off a request for a credit.

brrrr.title: BRRRR Rehab Contractor in Lexington, KY | Genstone
brrrr.metaDescription: BRRRR renovations in Lexington: Gardenside, Cardinal Valley, Meadowthorpe and Southland ranches rehabbed to appraise for refinance and built for tenants.
brrrr.intro: Lexington's limited land supply tends to keep values inside the Urban Service Boundary firm, which helps BRRRR investors when the refinance appraisal comes in. The challenge is buying low enough in a competitive market and keeping the renovation focused on what appraisers and tenants value. Most of our Lexington BRRRR clients target post-war ranches and modest homes in Gardenside, Cardinal Valley, Meadowthorpe, Southland, Lansdowne and Eastland, where rental demand is steady and comps are consistent. Genstone Construction plans those projects around both the appraisal and long-term durability. Our free Pre-Offer Rehab Review estimates repairs and compares them with likely after-repair value. For the refinance step, Genstone Financial, part of the same group of companies, offers DSCR rental loans.

sections.h2: Renovating to the Lexington refinance appraisal
sections.body:
A Fayette County appraiser values a renovated rental against recent sales of similar homes nearby, so the scope should match the better-maintained comps on that street. For a 1950s brick ranch in Gardenside or Meadowthorpe, that typically means a sound roof, updated electrical panel, working furnace and central air, a clean kitchen with durable counters, an updated bath, consistent flooring and fresh paint. Homes in Cardinal Valley or Eastland may need similar work with added attention to drainage and crawlspaces.

Appraisers in Lexington generally recognize updated systems, kitchens, baths and the absence of deferred maintenance. They are less likely to give full credit for high-end tile, custom cabinetry or elaborate landscaping in rental-grade neighborhoods. We keep the scope aligned with what the comps support.

Every renovation is documented with dated photos, permits, inspections and an itemized list of replaced systems and finishes. That package helps the appraiser and lender understand the work, especially when the online listing still shows the home before renovation.

sections.h2: Built for Lexington tenants and weather
sections.body:
After the refinance, the property has to perform as a rental. Lexington's humid summers make air conditioning essential, so HVAC systems are sized for the house, ductwork is sealed and condensate lines are routed to drain reliably. Crawlspaces get vapor barriers and drainage corrections where needed, because damp crawlspaces lead to odors, mold and soft floors that drive tenants out.

We favor luxury vinyl plank in main living areas, kitchens and baths, standard paint colors and sheens, durable counters and fixtures that can be replaced quickly. Gutters and downspouts are repaired and extended to keep water away from foundations, and grading is corrected where water pools near the house. In older homes, a camera inspection of the sewer lateral and a backwater valve can prevent backups that damage tenant belongings.

For pre-1978 homes, lead-safe work practices apply, and owners leasing to households with housing assistance should expect lead-related inspections. Durable, dry and simple rentals keep maintenance costs down and protect the cash flow that justified the BRRRR strategy.

The strongest Lexington BRRRR candidates are structurally sound homes in neighborhoods with steady rental demand and consistent comparable sales. Post-war ranches in Gardenside, Cardinal Valley, Meadowthorpe, Southland, Lansdowne and Eastland often fit because their structure is straightforward and their rents are predictable.

Older homes in Kenwick, the North Side or near campus can also work, but they usually carry more system and foundation costs, and some face historic overlay review for exterior changes. Homes near mapped sinkholes or with active foundation movement need an engineer's review before purchase. Properties with unpermitted basement or attic bedrooms, common near the university, may need egress or layout changes before they can be rented legally and appraised fully.

We flag those issues during the Pre-Offer Rehab Review. In a competitive market, it is tempting to stretch on price, but a house whose repair cost leaves little equity can trap capital for years. If the numbers do not support a refinance, we will tell you, and we may suggest a different strategy or a different property.

faqs.q: Can Genstone coordinate the refinance on a Lexington BRRRR?
faqs.a: Genstone Construction handles the renovation. Genstone Financial, a sister company within the Genstone Companies, provides DSCR rental loans along with fix-and-flip loans and lines of credit. Any lender works with us, but if you want the rehab documentation and refinance underwriting aligned, we can introduce you to Genstone Financial before you close on the Lexington property. In a market where good houses go quickly, having the refinance conversation early lets you move with confidence.

faqs.q: What Lexington neighborhoods work best for BRRRR?
faqs.a: Post-war neighborhoods such as Gardenside, Cardinal Valley, Meadowthorpe, Southland, Lansdowne and Eastland often combine steady rental demand with consistent comps. Older homes closer to downtown can work too, but they often require more foundation, drainage and system work. We review the specific property, nearby sales and rents during the Pre-Offer Rehab Review before you buy, and point out when the comps on that street are too thin to support the loan you need.

faqs.q: How do you document a Lexington BRRRR for the appraiser?
faqs.a: We provide dated before, during and after photos, an itemized list of replaced systems and finishes, and copies of permits and final inspections from the Division of Building Inspection. That package gives the appraiser and lender a clear picture of the renovation, which matters when public listing photos still show the home's pre-rehab condition. You can pass it along yourself, or we can send it straight to your loan officer.

rental-renovation.title: Rental Property Renovation in Lexington, KY | Genstone
rental-renovation.metaDescription: Single-family rental renovation in Lexington for portfolio owners: consistent specs, dry crawlspaces, sized HVAC, campus-area durability and tenant-ready turns.
rental-renovation.intro: Lexington rental portfolios often combine post-war ranches in Gardenside and Meadowthorpe, older bungalows near downtown and houses close to the University of Kentucky that see heavy student use. Each type wears differently, but owners still want consistent finishes, predictable costs and homes that lease quickly. Genstone Construction renovates single-family rentals across Lexington and Fayette County for individual investors, funds and portfolio owners. We stabilize newly acquired houses, take on bigger renovations between long-term residents, and hand routine turns to our sister company Genstone Field Services. Every project has a designated field manager, itemized pricing and photo documentation, so you can manage your Lexington rentals without being on site, whether you own two houses near campus or a few dozen ranches scattered across the north and south sides.

sections.h2: A rental standard for Lexington's mixed portfolio
sections.body:
Finishes are where consistency pays. Flooring, paint colors and sheens, cabinets, counters, plumbing fixtures, lighting and appliance packages can be the same in a Gardenside ranch, a Kenwick bungalow and a campus-area rental. Buying one set of products for every Lexington address shortens turns and lets a maintenance tech carry the right parts in the truck.

Structure and systems need a property-by-property approach. A post-war ranch may need a new panel, furnace, condenser and water heater. A prewar bungalow may need rewiring, new supply lines, a sewer lateral repair and foundation drainage. A house near campus may need egress corrections for basement or attic bedrooms, damaged doors and trim replaced and electrical circuits upgraded for heavy use. We write those differences into each scope so costs reflect real conditions.

Your standard should also include Lexington-specific durability items: properly sized air conditioning, sealed ducts, crawlspace vapor barriers, gutters and downspouts that move water away from foundations, and finishes tough enough for the student lease cycle in homes close to the university.

Homes near the University of Kentucky face a different kind of wear. Leases often turn over each year, several adults may share a house and common areas take a beating. Doors, trim, flooring, kitchens and bathrooms wear out faster than in a typical family rental.

We plan these renovations for heavy use. Solid-core doors and sturdy hardware hold up better than hollow doors. Luxury vinyl plank resists water and scratches. Kitchens get durable counters and cabinets with good hardware, and bathrooms use easy-to-clean surfaces with strong ventilation fans to prevent mold. Electrical systems may need additional circuits for multiple occupants and appliances.

Safety is a priority. Every sleeping room needs proper egress, and basement or attic bedrooms that were created without approval may need new windows, layout changes or a different use. Interconnected smoke alarms and carbon monoxide alarms are standard in our renovations. Zoning, occupancy rules and parking near campus should also be reviewed before purchase, because they affect how many tenants a property can legally serve.

sections.h2: Turns and ongoing care for Lexington owners
sections.body:
After stabilization, the focus shifts to keeping homes leased. Our sister company, Genstone Field Services, takes on that turn and make-ready work, along with inspections, occupied maintenance and code compliance.

A Lexington turn starts with a photographed move-out walkthrough, followed by a scope priced against your rental standard and repairs by vetted Fayette County contractors. Standard materials make matching paint, flooring and fixtures straightforward. Photos of damage support deposit decisions and build a history of each property.

Near campus, turns tend to cluster around the end of the academic year, so we plan labor and materials ahead to complete multiple houses in a short window. For family rentals elsewhere, turns are a good time to check HVAC filters, condensate drains, crawlspace moisture and gutters before small issues become expensive. Genstone's one-year workmanship warranty covers renovation work we performed, while tenant damage and normal wear are handled within the turn scope. Your property manager can coordinate access and tenant communication while you follow scopes, approvals and progress remotely.

faqs.q: Can you renovate occupied Lexington rentals?
faqs.a: Yes. Occupied work is scheduled with notice, confined to defined areas and planned so tenants keep a working kitchen, bath and climate control whenever possible. In summer, air conditioning work is scheduled to minimize downtime. Genstone Field Services can also handle occupied maintenance, so smaller repairs between renovations do not require another vendor or a separate set of instructions. Tenants are told in advance who is coming and roughly how long each visit will take.

faqs.q: How do you handle the end-of-semester turn rush near UK?
faqs.a: We plan ahead. Once you know which campus-area leases are ending, we schedule walkthroughs, order standard materials and line up crews so multiple homes can be turned in a short window. Photos and scopes are sent for approval quickly. That helps owners get houses ready for the next lease term without paying for long vacancies or rushed, inconsistent work. Houses that need larger repairs are flagged early so they can be started first.

faqs.q: How do you price renovations across a Lexington portfolio?
faqs.a: Each property gets an itemized estimate, with finishes and many line items coming from your portfolio standard. Structural, drainage and system work is priced house by house based on age and condition. Dumpster and debris costs are included in every estimate, and draws follow completed work, so you can compare costs across properties and track progress clearly, including why a campus duplex costs more to turn than a Southland ranch.

multifamily-renovation.title: Duplex & 2-4 Unit Renovation in Lexington, KY | Genstone
multifamily-renovation.metaDescription: Lexington duplex and small multifamily renovation: UK-area duplexes, divided older homes and fourplexes, with egress, fire separation and separate utilities.
multifamily-renovation.intro: Small multifamily properties in Lexington cluster around the University of Kentucky and the older neighborhoods near downtown. Investors find side-by-side and up-and-down duplexes in Aylesford, Columbia Heights and the streets off Euclid and Limestone, large Victorian and early twentieth-century homes divided into apartments on the North Side and in South Hill, and newer duplexes and fourplexes from the 1970s and 1980s in neighborhoods farther out. These buildings can offer several rents on one lot, but they raise questions about legal unit count, egress, fire separation, utilities and historic overlays. Genstone Construction renovates two- to four-unit properties in Lexington with those questions answered first. Our free Pre-Offer Rehab Review prices the work before you commit.

sections.h2: Campus duplexes and divided older homes
sections.body:
Many multifamily properties near the University of Kentucky have been rented for decades, and their condition reflects that. Typical findings include worn floors and kitchens, damaged doors and trim, overloaded electrical circuits, basement or attic bedrooms without proper egress and units added without approval. Older homes on the North Side and in South Hill may have been divided long ago, with shared utilities, a single stairway serving upper units and limited fire separation.

Before buying, confirm the legal unit count through LFUCG records and compare it with the current layout. From there, the renovation can bring the existing units up to current requirements, reduce the count to something that can be legitimized and financed, or convert the building to single-family use where owner-occupant demand supports it. Each path has different costs and income potential, and we price them side by side.

Many of these neighborhoods fall within H-1 historic overlays. Exterior changes such as new stairs, windows, porches or siding may require a Certificate of Appropriateness, which we build into the schedule.

Safety work is often the core of a Lexington multifamily renovation. When walls and ceilings are opened, inspectors from the Division of Building Inspection may require upgrades in the work area. Typical items include fire-rated assemblies between units, sealed penetrations, fire blocking in attics and chases, interconnected smoke alarms in every unit and carbon monoxide alarms near fuel-burning appliances.

Egress requires particular care near campus, where basement and attic rooms are often used as bedrooms. Each sleeping room needs a compliant escape route, which may mean enlarging windows, adding window wells or changing how rooms are used. Upper units served by one stairway may need a second exit.

Utility separation affects both income and management. Separate electric and gas meters and independent HVAC systems let tenants pay their own utilities and control their own comfort. That can require new services from Kentucky Utilities and Columbia Gas, upgraded panels and new ductwork. We price separation as a distinct line item so you can compare it with expected rents before deciding.

Many Lexington multifamily buyers inherit tenants, and near campus leases often run on the academic calendar. That timing can be an advantage. When several units turn over at the end of the school year, the summer window gives a chance to complete bigger renovations before the next lease term begins.

Where units stay occupied, we phase the work. Vacant units are renovated first, and occupied units follow as leases end or tenants move. Whole-building work such as roofing, electrical service upgrades, gas line replacement, sewer lateral repair or HVAC changes is scheduled with notice and kept as short as possible. Occupied units keep air conditioning through Lexington summers and heat through the winter months.

Shared areas are cleaned and secured daily. Your field manager coordinates tenant communication through your property manager, documents each phase with photos and closes permits and inspections before moving to the next stage. That approach keeps the building generating rent while it improves, and it gives lenders and insurers a clear record of completed work.

faqs.q: Are duplexes near the University of Kentucky good investments?
faqs.a: Many do well, because demand from students, staff and UK HealthCare employees is persistent. The risk sits in the details: zoning, occupancy rules, parking and neighborhood expectations all need checking, and plenty of campus-area properties carry heavy wear or bedrooms that were never permitted. We evaluate condition, egress, safety items and likely renovation cost during the Pre-Offer Rehab Review so you can judge the deal on real numbers.

faqs.q: How do I confirm the legal unit count in a Lexington building?
faqs.a: Start with LFUCG permit and zoning records and compare them with the building's current layout. Property valuation records and older listings can provide clues but are not definitive. If the records support fewer units than exist, we can price the work to legitimize them where zoning allows or a plan to reduce the count, so you know the options before purchase.

faqs.q: Can I renovate a campus-area building during the summer break?
faqs.a: Often, yes, and it is one of the best times to do it. When leases end in spring, several units may be vacant at once, giving room for larger renovations before the next term. We plan materials and crews ahead so work can begin as soon as tenants move out, with the goal of having units ready for new leases.

fha-203k.title: FHA 203(k) Contractor in Lexington, KY | Genstone
fha-203k.metaDescription: FHA 203(k) certified contractor in Lexington: Standard and Limited bids for Kenwick bungalows, post-war ranches and owner-occupied duplexes, with draw support.
fha-203k.intro: In a tight market like Lexington, an FHA 203(k) loan can open doors for buyers who would otherwise be outbid on move-in-ready homes. It lets a buyer purchase a house that needs work and finance the renovation in the same mortgage, which suits Lexington's older bungalows in Kenwick and the North Side and its post-war ranches in Gardenside, Meadowthorpe and Southland. Genstone Construction is FHA 203(k) certified, and for that kind of purchase we produce the itemized bids, scopes and draw schedules lenders and consultants require, then manage the renovation to completion. Buyers, agents and loan officers in Fayette County work with us to keep 203(k) transactions organized and on schedule.

sections.body:
For nonstructural work, the Limited 203(k) allows total rehabilitation costs up to $75,000. Once a project passes $15,000, an inspection is required; below that, the lender decides whether to require one. A 203(k) consultant is optional on Limited loans, though some lenders ask for one. In Lexington, the Limited version often fits a Meadowthorpe or Southland ranch that needs a new HVAC system, roof, flooring and kitchen updates, or a bungalow that needs paint, windows and a bathroom refresh.

The Standard 203(k) is designed for larger or structural renovations. It requires rehabilitation costs of at least $5,000 and an FHA-approved 203(k) consultant. That route is usually better for a Kenwick or North Side home with foundation and drainage problems, full rewiring, plumbing replacement, crawlspace structural repair or a reconfigured layout.

We walk the house with the buyer and agent and recommend the version that matches the real scope. Forcing a foundation or structural job into the Limited program typically creates problems later in the transaction.

sections.h2: Lexington homes that work well with a 203(k)
sections.body:
The best Lexington 203(k) candidates are homes with significant but clearly defined problems. A Kenwick bungalow with knob-and-tube wiring and a damp basement, a Gardenside ranch with an aging roof and failing HVAC, or a North Side cottage with peeling lead paint and outdated plumbing can all fit the program well.

Drainage and foundations deserve early attention. Homes near mapped karst features or with visible settlement may need an engineer's review. Basements and crawlspaces with seepage or moisture problems may need drainage, sump pumps or vapor barriers. Identifying those items early ensures the loan amount covers them.

Historic overlays matter too. Homes in Bell Court, South Hill, Aylesford or other H-1 districts may need a Certificate of Appropriateness for exterior changes, which should be built into the timeline.

FHA also allows owner-occupied properties with two to four units. A buyer could purchase a duplex near campus, live in one unit and renovate the building with 203(k) financing, provided the unit count, egress and fire separation are in order.

Lenders on a 203(k) typically require a detailed contractor bid organized by line item and matched to the consultant's work write-up, along with licensing and insurance documentation. We prepare bids in that format and revise them quickly when the appraiser, consultant or underwriter asks for changes.

After closing, renovation funds are held in escrow and paid out in draws as work is completed and inspected. Our field manager schedules the project so each draw lines up with a clear milestone, collects lien waivers from trades and coordinates permits with LFUCG's Division of Building Inspection and state-licensed trades.

Lead-safe practices apply to homes built before 1978, which includes most of Lexington's older housing. When hidden conditions appear after demolition, such as rotted sills, deteriorated wiring or a cracked lateral, we document them and follow the lender's change-order process so contingency funds are used properly. Buyers can follow each milestone, and the final payment is made only after the work is complete and they approve it.

faqs.q: Can a 203(k) cover basement drainage in a Lexington home?
faqs.a: Yes, if the work is included in the approved scope. Grading, drainage systems, sump pumps, crack repair and crawlspace vapor barriers can all be part of a 203(k) renovation. Because water problems are common in older Lexington homes, we recommend identifying them during the walkthrough so the bid and loan amount include the necessary work from the start. Homes near mapped sinkholes may also need an engineer's letter.

faqs.q: Does a historic overlay complicate a 203(k) in Lexington?
faqs.a: It adds a step but does not prevent the loan. In H-1 districts, exterior changes such as windows, siding, porches and roofing usually need a Certificate of Appropriateness. We confirm overlay status early, plan exterior work to fit district guidelines and build review time into the schedule so it does not delay closing or the first draw. Interior work usually needs no overlay review at all.

faqs.q: Can I use a 203(k) to buy a duplex near UK?
faqs.a: Yes, if you will live in one unit and the property is eligible. Owner-occupied buildings of up to four units are eligible under FHA. Campus-area duplexes often need egress improvements, fire separation, utility separation and heavy-wear repairs, so we review those items carefully. Your lender confirms eligibility and how rent from the second unit is counted. Unpermitted basement bedrooms are a common issue we flag early.

reo-renovation.title: REO & Bank-Owned Renovation in Lexington | Genstone
reo-renovation.metaDescription: REO renovation in Lexington for servicers, banks and GSEs: moisture, mold, freeze damage, code cases and disposition-ready repairs on vacant Fayette homes.
reo-renovation.h1: REO and Bank-Owned Property Renovations in Lexington
reo-renovation.intro: Bank-owned homes are less common in Lexington than in many Midwest and Kentucky markets, partly because tight supply keeps buyers active. When an REO property does appear, speed matters, because a well-prepared house can sell quickly while a neglected one sits and deteriorates. Vacant homes here face humidity, damp crawlspaces, mold, storm damage and occasional freeze damage, along with code enforcement cases. Genstone Construction renovates REO properties in Lexington and Fayette County for mortgage servicers, banks, REITs, investment funds and Government-Sponsored Enterprises, and Genstone is a preferred contractor for GSE work. Through our sister company Genstone Field Services, one organization can secure, inspect, maintain and renovate the property from first visit to disposition.

sections.h2: What vacant Lexington homes usually need
sections.body:
Moisture is the most common problem in Lexington REO properties. Closed homes without air conditioning trap humidity, and mold can develop on walls, ceilings, cabinets and crawlspace framing. Clay soils and poor drainage keep crawlspaces and basements damp, which can soften sills and joists. Homes near karst features may also show drainage patterns that are hard to predict.

Other conditions include roof leaks from storms, freeze-damaged plumbing after cold snaps, missing or damaged HVAC equipment, broken windows, debris and overgrown yards. Near campus, a former rental may show heavy tenant wear in addition to vacancy damage.

We begin with a full walkthrough, photographs of every room, the crawlspace and the attic, and a pressure test of any remaining plumbing. Missing systems are documented for replacement. We also confirm utility status, because Kentucky Utilities, Columbia Gas and Kentucky American Water may require repairs and inspections before service is restored. That early assessment helps asset managers decide quickly how to position the property.

sections.h2: Code enforcement, overlays and permits on Lexington REO
sections.body:
LFUCG's Division of Code Enforcement cites vacant properties for tall grass, debris, open structures, broken windows and unsafe conditions, and those cases can follow a property through foreclosure. Fines and abatement costs may also become liens.

Genstone Field Services handles code compliance work and coordinates with Genstone Construction so citations are addressed in the renovation plan. Permits for structural, electrical, plumbing and mechanical work are pulled through the Division of Building Inspection and the appropriate state-licensed trades, and each correction is documented so the case can be closed.

REO properties in H-1 historic districts such as Bell Court, South Hill or Aylesford may need a Certificate of Appropriateness before exterior repairs. That affects windows, siding, porches and roofing, and we build the review into the timeline. Homes near mapped sinkholes or with foundation movement may need engineering review before structural repairs. Clearing code issues and closing permits helps the property sell more smoothly and reduces the risk of new citations while it is listed.

Asset managers usually choose between a retail-ready renovation for owner-occupant buyers, financing-focused repairs that help the property qualify for FHA or conventional loans, or limited work that resolves health, safety and code issues before an investor sale. In Lexington's tight market, a retail-ready or financing-ready scope often makes sense because buyer demand is strong.

A retail-ready scope may include restoring HVAC, water and power, mold remediation, crawlspace moisture correction, roof repairs, new flooring and paint, kitchen and bath updates and exterior cleanup. A financing-focused scope targets items appraisers commonly flag, such as peeling paint on pre-1978 homes, missing handrails, inoperable systems or active leaks. A limited scope may focus on securing the property, removing debris and correcting hazards.

Haul-off and dumpster charges are already in the estimate, and the closeout file carries lien waivers along with before-and-after photos. A designated field manager stays with each Lexington property from first walkthrough through final billing, giving asset managers one point of contact for approvals, status and reporting.

faqs.q: Does Genstone provide preservation and renovation on Lexington REO?
faqs.a: Yes. Genstone Field Services handles property preservation, inspections, occupied maintenance, turn and make-ready work and code compliance, while Genstone Construction completes renovation. Keeping both within the Genstone Companies means one photo history and record set for each Lexington property, which simplifies reporting and reduces handoff problems for servicers and asset managers. Because REO listings are scarce in Lexington, that continuity also helps get a house to market while buyer interest is high.

faqs.q: How quickly can a Lexington REO be prepared for listing?
faqs.a: It depends on the scope and condition, but we move quickly because Lexington's tight market rewards properties that hit the market in good shape. Exterior cleanup, securing and code items often happen first, while interior scopes are approved and permits are pulled. Your field manager provides a realistic schedule after the initial walkthrough and updates it as work progresses, including any time needed for historic overlay review.

faqs.q: Can you clear code violations on bank-owned Lexington homes?
faqs.a: Yes. We review open cases with the asset manager, include corrective work in the scope, pull permits and provide photo documentation so each case can be closed. Exterior items such as mowing, debris removal and broken windows are usually handled first, which reduces the chance of new citations while interior work proceeds. If a property carries code liens, we flag them to the asset manager at the outset.
